title: CBI Files Chargesheet Against 17 in Rs 9,280-Crore Reliance ADA Fraud Case
excerpt: Three senior executives, eight group companies, and six bank officials named in supplementary chargesheet as India's largest corporate fraud probe widens.
body:
• CBI filed a supplementary chargesheet naming 17 more accused — including three Reliance ADA Group executives and eight group companies — in the Rs 9,280-crore Reliance Commercial Finance fraud case.
  • The agency alleges Rs 6,229.54 crore borrowed by RCFL was diverted through intermediary entities to various Reliance ADA Group companies, causing wrongful loss to 31 lenders.
  • With this filing, 24 individuals and companies have been chargesheeted across the case, while seven arrests have been made. The Supreme Court is monitoring the investigation.
  • The case is part of a broader probe involving eight FIRs against multiple Reliance ADA Group entities, based on complaints from public sector banks, LIC, and EPFO.

CBI Expands Net in Rs 9,280-Crore Fraud Case

The Central Bureau of Investigation on Monday filed a supplementary chargesheet against 17 more accused in the Reliance Commercial Finance Limited (RCFL) case, significantly widening the net in what has become one of the largest corporate fraud investigations in India.

The chargesheet, filed before the Special Judge for CBI cases in Mumbai, names three senior executives of the Anil Ambani-led Reliance ADA Group: Amitabh Jhunjhunwala, Group Managing Director; Amit Bapna, Chief Financial Officer of Reliance Capital Limited; and Ramesh Shenoy, Company Secretary of Reliance Infrastructure Ltd.

Eight Reliance ADA Group companies have also been listed as accused: Reliance Power Ltd., Big Flicks Pvt. Ltd., Reliance Big Entertainment Pvt. Ltd., Reliance Communications Ltd., Kunjbihari Developers Pvt. Ltd., Reliance Venture Asset Management Pvt. Ltd., Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd., and Reliance Telecom Ltd. Six bank officials from Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, and Indian Overseas Bank round out the list.

"RCFL was availing loans to the tune of Rs 9,280 crore from 31 banks, financial institutions, NBFCs and corporate bodies. A thorough investigation will be conducted into the allegations of defrauding all the lenders by the accused company."

— CBI statement

How the Alleged Diversion Worked

According to the CBI, Rs 6,229.54 crore borrowed by RCFL was diverted through intermediary and conduit entities to various Reliance ADA Group companies, allegedly violating the terms and conditions of the borrowings. The total estimated loss to banks, financial institutions, and other lenders stands at approximately Rs 9,280 crore (.1 billion).

The accused face charges including criminal conspiracy, criminal misappropriation, and cheating under the Indian Penal Code, along with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

A Broader Investigation Takes Shape

The RCFL case is part of a wider investigation into multiple Reliance ADA Group entities. The CBI's Banking Security and Fraud Branch in Delhi has registered eight FIRs against Reliance Communications, Reliance Home Finance, RCFL, Reliance Telecom, and other group companies, based on complaints from public sector banks, Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), and the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO).

The CBI had filed its first chargesheet in the RCFL case on July 7, 2026, against seven accused persons. With this supplementary filing — the sixth chargesheet across all Reliance ADA Group cases — a total of 24 individuals and companies have been chargesheeted. Seven accused have been arrested so far.

The investigation is being monitored by the Supreme Court, underscoring its significance in India's ongoing efforts to hold corporations accountable for financial fraud.

What It Means for Indian Financial Markets

The case highlights persistent concerns about corporate governance failures at conglomerate groups that borrowed heavily from public sector banks. The involvement of LIC and EPFO as complainants means that public savings — including retirement funds — were among the victims of the alleged fraud.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with investments in Indian markets or NRI deposits with public sector banks, the case raises important questions about the adequacy of oversight mechanisms for large corporate borrowers. The outcome of this investigation could set precedents for how India handles large-scale financial fraud involving publicly listed conglomerates.
